findings.body:
**Authorization removed on a destructive endpoint.** Deleting `@require_role("admin")` leaves `DELETE /users/<user>` with no access control — any caller can remove any user from `USERS` and get `204`.

Concrete failure mode: `curl -X DELETE /users/alice` (no auth) succeeds and drops `alice` from the in-memory user list. Cleanup jobs getting 403 as `viewer` means those jobs lack the right role; they should authenticate as a principal that is allowed to delete (service account / admin), or use a separate authenticated internal cleanup path.

Restoring a caller-based admin check (from session/token, not the path `<user>`) is the minimum fix; do not ship an open delete.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change removes the only authorization check on `DELETE /users/<user>`, turning a privileged destructive endpoint into a fully open delete API.

## Findings

| # | Severity | File | Summary |
|---|----------|------|---------|
| 1 | 🚨 critical | `app.py:19` | AuthZ decorator removed; anyone can delete any user |

## Analysis

The PR drops `@require_role("admin")` from `delete_user` because cleanup jobs running as the viewer account were getting 403s. That is an authorization failure being “fixed” by removing authorization.

After this change, any client can call `DELETE /users/<user>` with no role gate and mutate the shared `USERS` list (204 on success). That is a broken access-control / IDOR-class failure on a destructive route.

The cleanup-job 403 needs a dedicated identity and role (or a separate internal cleanup path with real service auth), not a public unauthenticated delete.

Note on adjacent context (not a new inline finding): `require_role` currently compares `ROLES.get(user)` where `user` is the *path* target, not the caller. Even before this PR the check was misfocused; removing it entirely is still a strict regression to no checks at all.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes
